name: Serum osmolality
seoDesc: Serum osmolality: work out serum osmolality from the blood urea nitrogen and the glucose. A free health calculator with the formula, units and a worked…
summary: Give the Serum osmolality calculator the blood urea nitrogen, the glucose, the serum alcohol concetration and the measured serum osmolality and it returns serum osmolality. It is built for an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. Editing anything puts the results away until the next press of Calculate — change one value at a time and the updated answer tells you what that value was worth.

sections.title: How does the Serum osmolality calculator work?
sections.html:
The Serum osmolality calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports serum osmolality in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the blood urea nitrogen, the glucose, the serum alcohol concetration and the measured serum osmolality.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A number, expressed in mEq/L.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in milligrams per deciliter. The unit chip switches it to any of the 5 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in milligrams per decilitre. The unit chip switches it to any of the 2 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in millimoles per liter. The unit chip switches it to any of the 2 supported units.
  • A number, expressed in mOsm/kg H₂O.

sections.title: The formula behind the Serum osmolality calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Serum osmolality=((5 ÷ 14) × blood urea nitrogen + 2 × na + (10 ÷ 37) × serum alcohol concetration + (1 ÷ 18) × glucose)
Osmotic gap=(measured serum osmolality − ((5 ÷ 14) × blood urea nitrogen + 2 × na + (10 ÷ 37) × serum alcohol concetration + (1 ÷ 18) × glucose))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Na = 10, Blood urea nitrogen = 10 Mg/d l, Glucose = 10 Mg/d l and Serum alcohol concetration = 10 mmol/L. Working through the relationship above gives Serum osmolality = 27 and Osmotic gap = -17.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Serum osmolality = 27 and Osmotic gap = -17 should be roughly the size you expected from Na = 10 and Blood urea nitrogen = 10 Mg/d l.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Urea, opening in milligrams per deciliter
  • Glucose levels, opening in milligrams per decilitre
  • Serum alcohol concentration, opening in millimoles per liter

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Serum osmolality calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the blood urea nitrogen, the glucose and the serum alcohol concetration — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Serum osmolality calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The unit chips cover the units listed on the page. A historical or regional unit that is missing can still be used by converting it to a listed unit first.
  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

faq.q: What does the Serum osmolality calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns serum osmolality, derived from the blood urea nitrogen, the glucose and the serum alcohol concetration. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Serum osmolality calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the blood urea nitrogen, the glucose, the serum alcohol concetration and the measured serum osmolality, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter blood urea nitrogen in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Blood urea nitrogen opens in milligrams per deciliter and the chip beside it offers 5 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Serum osmolality = 27. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Serum osmolality calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
